Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Kofi's eyes still widened in fear when he recalled the day his doctor told him he had stage IV cancer. It felt like it was happening right now, not two years ago. The numbness that initially enveloped him after the diagnosis slowly gave way to an overwhelming sense of dread every time the memory resurfaced. He would be sitting at his desk, reviewing policy briefs as a senior analyst, when suddenly he'd feel like he was back in that cold hospital room, hearing those devastating words. As Kofi struggled to shake off the memories, he became increasingly convinced that his body had turned against him. The constant tension in his muscles, the feeling of being on high alert even in his own home, all seemed to confirm this terrible suspicion. His body felt like a ticking time bomb, waiting to unleash another life-threatening crisis at any moment. He started to avoid certain tasks and situations that reminded him of his illness, like visiting friends who were also dealing with health issues or going for long walks alone. As he began to withdraw from social interactions, Kofi's feelings of isolation deepened. His wife had passed away a few years before his diagnosis, and without her support system, he felt lost and adrift. He became convinced that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again - the fear and anxiety had taken over, and he couldn't shake them off. Kofi's body seemed to be constantly on edge, as if waiting for another blow to strike. His mind racing with worst-case scenarios, he found himself repeatedly checking his vital signs, searching for any sign of trouble brewing. This hyper-vigilance only served to heighten his sense of threat, which in turn made the memories of his diagnosis even more unbearable. As Kofi's world shrunk, so did his ability to concentrate on his work. He was no longer able to focus on the intricate policy analyses that had once been his passion. The tension and anxiety had taken over, making it hard for him to sit still or quiet his mind long enough to complete even simple tasks. One day, while reviewing a particularly complex brief, Kofi's hand began shaking uncontrollably as he scribbled notes on the margin. He froze, staring at his trembling fingers in horror - was this another symptom of something going terribly wrong? The wave of fear washed over him, and for a moment, he was back in that hospital room again. It was then that Kofi realized he needed help to break free from this cycle of dread and anxiety. His fears about his body's reliability, the constant threat lurking around every corner - these thoughts had become an all-consuming force in his life. He scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping that she could help him rebuild some semblance of control over his emotions and his life. As he sat waiting for their first session to begin, Kofi's mind racing with worries about what might happen next, he couldn't shake the feeling that time was running out - for him, and for any chance at reclaiming a sense of peace.
